steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the section on integrated local APICs for an encyclopedia article on the Advanced Programmable Interrupt Controller: what local APICs do, which processors have them, how they relate to MSI, and a subsection on the APIC timer.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- What local APICs do
- Which Intel processors have one built in
- Local APIC and MSI
- APIC timer (subsection): features, early criticism, use in Windows and Linux

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Role
  - LAPICs manage all external interrupts for a specific processor in an SMP system
  - accept and generate inter-processor interrupts (IPIs) between LAPICs
  - up to 224 usable interrupt vectors from an I/O APIC; vectors 0 to 31 (of 0 to 255) reserved for x86 exception handling
- Processors
  - all Intel processors from P5 microarchitecture (P54C) have built-in local APIC
  - P5: if disabled, cannot be re-enabled by software; not a limitation in P6 and later
  - Pentium 4 HT and Pentium D: each core and each thread has integrated LAPIC
- MSI
  - Message Signaled Interrupts (PCI 2.2 and later) need the local APIC enabled
  - MSI obviates need for I/O APIC; up to 224 interrupts in MSI mode; no IRQ sharing
- APIC timer
  - high-resolution (about one microsecond or better), interval and one-off mode
  - initial acceptance woes: Microsoft document from 2002 (pushing High Precision Event Timer) criticized "poor resolution", "the clocks silicon is sometimes very buggy"
  - used by Windows 7 when profiling enabled, Windows 8 always; before Windows 8 took exclusive rights, used by programs like CPU-Z; not shareable under Windows
  - Linux tickless kernel uses its aperiodic interrupts; optional but default, new with 2.6.18; kernel then does not use the 8253 programmable interval timer for timekeeping
  - [quote: VMware document on determining the timer's frequency]

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Local APICs (LAPICs) manage all of the external interrupts for some specific processor in an SMP system. They can also accept and generate inter-processor interrupts (IPIs) between LAPICs. One LAPIC may support up to 224 usable interrupt vectors from an I/O APIC. The vector numbers 0 to 31, out of 0 to 255, are reserved for exception handling by x86 processors.

All Intel processors starting with the P5 microarchitecture (P54C) have a local APIC built in. But if the local APIC is disabled in a P5 processor, software cannot re-enable it. This limitation is not there anymore in the P6 processors and the ones after them.

When the Pentium 4 HT and Pentium D were introduced, each CPU core and each CPU thread have the integrated LAPIC.

- MSI (PCI 2.2 and later) needs local APIC enabled; obviates I/O APIC; up to 224 interrupts in MSI mode; no IRQ sharing

### APIC timer

- high-resolution (one microsecond or better), interval and one-off mode
- initial acceptance woes: 2002 Microsoft document (for High Precision Event Timer) — "poor resolution", "the clocks silicon is sometimes very buggy"
- used by Windows 7 when profiling, Windows 8 always; CPU-Z before that; not shareable under Windows
- Linux tickless kernel, optional but default, new with 2.6.18; then no 8253 PIT for timekeeping
- VMware quote: "software does not have a reliable way to determine its frequency. Generally, the only way to determine the local APIC timer’s frequency is to measure it using the PIT or CMOS timer, which yields only an approximate result."

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Local APICs (LAPICs) manage all of the external interrupts for some specific processor in an SMP system. They can also accept and generate inter-processor interrupts (IPIs) between LAPICs. One LAPIC may support up to 224 usable interrupt vectors from an I/O APIC. The vector numbers 0 to 31, out of 0 to 255, are reserved for exception handling by x86 processors.

All Intel processors starting with the P5 microarchitecture (P54C) have a local APIC built in. But if the local APIC is disabled in a P5 processor, software cannot re-enable it. This limitation is not there anymore in the P6 processors and the ones after them.

When the Pentium 4 HT and Pentium D were introduced, each CPU core and each CPU thread have the integrated LAPIC.

The Message Signaled Interrupts (MSI) feature of the PCI 2.2 and later specifications can't be used unless the local APIC is enabled. Using MSI obviates the need for an I/O APIC. Also, up to 224 interrupts are supported in MSI mode, and IRQ sharing is not allowed.

### APIC timer

The local APIC has another advantage, which is that it also provides a high-resolution timer (on the order of one microsecond or better) that can be used in both interval and one-off mode.

At first the APIC timer had some problems getting accepted. A Microsoft document from 2002, which advocated adopting the High Precision Event Timer instead, criticized the LAPIC timer for having "poor resolution" and stated that "the clocks silicon is sometimes very buggy". But the APIC timer is still used, for example by Windows 7 when profiling is enabled, and by Windows 8 in all circumstances. Before Windows 8 claimed exclusive rights to this timer, some programs like CPU-Z also used it. The APIC timer is not a shareable resource under Microsoft Windows.

The Linux kernel tickless kernel feature uses the aperiodic interrupts that the APIC timer offers. This feature is optional but default, and it is new with 2.6.18. When it is enabled on a computer that has an APIC timer, the kernel does not use the 8253 programmable interval timer for timekeeping. A VMware document notes that "software does not have a reliable way to determine its frequency. Generally, the only way to determine the local APIC timer’s frequency is to measure it using the PIT or CMOS timer, which yields only an approximate result."
